solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sent round specimens essentially taken as given

indicators.note: round says the mailing word goes around the picked letter

parts.note: sent by mail means posted

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so the central letter of specimens is taken

explanation.surface: Someone mails out samples that everyone simply assumes are genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts the central I of specimens inside POSTED.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit is to assume or put forward as fact, so something posited is assumed without proof.

clue.text: Coppers not completely holding me up in controversy

indicators.note: holding says the shortened police word wraps around the turned me
not completely means the last letter is cut from the police word

parts.note: coppers is slang for the police

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word me is read upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: Officers caught in a row over holding someone in custody.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' turns the little word over to give EM; 'Coppers' are police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a fierce verbal or written attack, a piece of heated controversy.

clue.text: A person readily welcoming me heading committee at last

indicators.note: heading means going in front of, so the combined letters precede the final letter
welcoming means taking in, so the word for readily goes around me

parts.note: as soon means as readily, so soon can stand for readily

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of committee

explanation.surface: Someone happily lets me chair the committee in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'readily' gives SOON as in 'I would as soon', meaning as willingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone means an unspecified individual, any one person.

clue.text: Head-to-toe cover for garment?

indicators.note: head-to-toe means the top letter of a down entry goes to the foot

parts.note: to strew is to scatter so as to cover a surface

explanation.surface: Asks whether a full-body wrap counts as a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head-to-toe' looks like describing an outfit, but moves the S of STREW from top to bottom. TREWS are close-fitting tartan trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Trews are tartan trousers worn in Scotland, so a garment.

clue.text: Notice southern girl wearing ring

indicators.note: wearing says the phone word is put on around the other letters

parts.note: to ring is to phone, which once meant to dial
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A southern girl's engagement ring gets noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' looks like jewellery being worn, but is the phone sense; 'Notice' is the definition, as in being given notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Being given notice means being told your job is ending, being fired.

clue.text: Ignoring nurse initially, doctor inspects dirty pool

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the remaining letters are rearranged
ignoring something leaves it out, so a letter is dropped from the following word
initially points to the opening letter of nurse

explanation.surface: A hospital doctor, bypassing the nurse, looks into a filthy pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctor' looks like a person but is the anagram signal; drop N from INSPECTS to leave ISPECTS, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A cesspit is a pit collecting sewage and waste, a literally dirty pool of liquid.

clue.text: Day in custody cell

indicators.note: in says the day letter goes inside the custody word

parts.note: custody, as of a child, is care

explanation.surface: Someone spends a day locked in a custody cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cell' looks like a prison room but means a small group.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadre is a small core group of trained activists, like a cell within a movement.

clue.text: Curiously subtler and almost petty

indicators.note: curiously means in an odd manner, so the letters are oddly rearranged
almost means not quite all, so the last letter of and is dropped

explanation.surface: Something oddly more subtle yet almost trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims AND to AN; 'Curiously' rearranges SUBTLER plus AN.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, subaltern means of lower rank or subordinate, so minor or petty.

clue.text: Rising up circling former top of ancient tableland

indicators.note: circling says the turned word surrounds the other letters
in a down clue, rising means the word up is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: late means former, as in the late president

indicators.note: top of picks the first letter of ancient

explanation.surface: Climbing up and round an old summit on a high plain.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'Rising' turns the little word to read PU.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is an area of high, flat ground, which is what tableland means.

clue.text: Most trim little flier expires trapped inside

indicators.note: trapped inside says the dying word is held within the bird

parts.note: a tit is a small bird
expires means dies

explanation.surface: A tiny, neat bird dies caught in a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim means neat and orderly, so most trim is the neatest.

clue.text: Exposed unctuous favourites and hangers-on

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters of the synonym go

parts.note: unctuous, oily and ingratiating, means slimy
favourites, such as a teacher's darlings, are pets

explanation.surface: Smarmy teacher's pets and their fawning followers are shown up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' strips the first and last letters from SLIMY, leaving LIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellfish that cling tightly to rocks give a figurative term for people who cling to others for advantage.

clue.text: Exceptional band had very able performer

indicators.note: exceptional means out of the ordinary, so the letters of band had are put out of their usual order

explanation.surface: An outstanding group of musicians had a gifted star in its line-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A dab hand is an idiom for someone highly skilled at a particular task, an expert.

clue.text: Tipsily homes in on foolish talk

indicators.note: tipsily means in a drunken, unsteady way, so the letters of homes in on stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunk zeroes in unsteadily on some nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the word also means illicit liquor, matching the drunken signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonshine is used informally for nonsense or fanciful, unrealistic talk.

clue.text: Relative position, say, about subject

parts.note: the lie of something is how it lies, its position relative to its surroundings

indicators.note: about signals turning the example abbreviation round

parts.note: say, as in 'for example', is abbreviated to e.g.

explanation.surface: A family member's stance on some topic is under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative' tempts as a family member, but 'Relative position' together gives LIE, as in the lie of the land.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal usage the word can mean a vassal owing allegiance, someone subject to a lord.

clue.text: Occasionally scarce farm product

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of scarce farm is taken

explanation.surface: A farm's output is sometimes in short supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' takes the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of 'scarce farm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimmed from milk, this dairy item is one of the things a farm turns out.

clue.text: Violent turmoil as merlot mixed with last of rum

indicators.note: mixed means jumbled, so these letters are put in a new order
last of picks the final letter of rum

explanation.surface: A bar's chaos as red wine is mixed with rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' looks like a link word, but its letters are part of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A maelstrom is a powerful whirlpool, used for any state of violent confusion.

clue.text: With singular speed, furnish high-altitude gear

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
speed means pace
to suit is to fit out or provide with what is needed, to furnish

explanation.surface: A climber is quickly kitted out for the heights.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronauts wear a pressurised outfit to survive at extreme altitude and in outer space.

clue.text: Scratchy things as with undergarments I've taken in

indicators.note: taken in says the underwear and the contraction go inside the word as

parts.note: bras are undergarments

explanation.surface: Sounds like itchy underwear I've had to take in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' looks like a link word but is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrasives are rough materials such as sandpaper that scratch or wear surfaces down.

clue.text: Driving mechanism to sustain vendors with no restrictions

parts.note: to prop is to hold up or support, to sustain

indicators.note: restrictions are limits, so the word loses its limiting outer letters

parts.note: vendors are sellers

explanation.surface: A mechanism meant to support traders operating in a free market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no restrictions' sounds like free trade, but removes the end letters of SELLERS to leave ELLER.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw of rotating blades drives a ship or aircraft forward, so it is a driving mechanism.

clue.text: Popular credit card, it's turning up in town, say, mostly

indicators.note: in says the turned letters go inside the shortened place word
mostly means most of it, so the final letter of the place word is dropped

parts.note: a town is an example of a place

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word it's is read upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: A well-used card turns up somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'turning up' reads the little word upwards, giving STI.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastic is informal for credit cards, the everyday way people pay.

clue.text: Part of record in a Latin service book

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Mentions a Latin record found within a prayer book.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinal is a church book setting out the order of services, especially ordinations.

clue.text: Jog in the altogether round centre of Rugby

indicators.note: round says the naked word goes around the middle letter

parts.note: in the altogether is an idiom for naked, nude

indicators.note: centre of picks the middle letter of the five-letter word Rugby

explanation.surface: A streaker runs naked around a rugby pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts the G from the middle of Rugby inside NUDE. Streakers famously run onto rugby pitches.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone is to give them a light push or poke, a gentle prod.

clue.text: Heard plan for a drink

indicators.note: heard says the word for plan is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a draft is a preliminary plan or version

explanation.surface: Someone overhears a scheme to go for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: In British spelling the drink is spelt differently from the plan, though both say the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught is a single swallow of liquid, a drink or dose.

clue.text: Tree with lowered resistance, in consequence put down

indicators.note: in says the altered tree goes inside the word for consequence

parts.note: an end is an outcome or consequence

indicators.note: in a down clue, lowered means the letter for resistance moves further down the word

parts.note: taken as the word tree
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: A tree with poor resistance is consequently felled.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'lowered' moves R one place further down, making TERE.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something down is to write it in a record, to log it officially.

clue.text: Range in Switzerland especially

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words Switzerland especially, across the join

explanation.surface: Suggests the Alps are found chiefly in Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the Alps, but the mountains hidden here are in South America.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the long chain of mountains running down the western side of South America.

clue.text: Law-abiding ordinary, second-class employee

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
B is the grade below A, so second-class
a servant is someone employed to serve

explanation.surface: Describes a humdrum, second-rate worker who obeys every rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Being observant can mean diligently keeping rules or religious law, so obedient to it.

clue.text: Curiously evenly folded clays

indicators.note: evenly means taking the even-numbered letters of folded clays

explanation.surface: Clays oddly folded neatly together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evenly' takes letters 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 of 'folded clays'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something done in a strange or unexpected way.

clue.text: Limits of country estate with first of gardeners gone

indicators.note: gone means departed, so the picked letter leaves the estate word

parts.note: a grange is a country house with farm buildings

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of gardeners

explanation.surface: The boundaries of a country estate after the head gardener leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone' removes G from GRANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is the extent between limits, as in a price range.

clue.text: Toughened after time with permanent post

indicators.note: after puts the hardened word behind the time letter

parts.note: enured, a variant of inured, means hardened or toughened

explanation.surface: Someone hardened by years of service finally lands a permanent job.
explanation.definitionFit: An academic with tenure holds a secure, permanent appointment.

clue.text: Storm about backing foreign plonk, sour stuff

indicators.note: backing means supporting from behind, so the turned word comes after the wine

parts.note: vin is French for wine, plonk being cheap wine

indicators.note: about signals turning the word for storm round

parts.note: to storm is to rage

explanation.surface: Someone rants about the cheap foreign wine, calling it sour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses RAGE to EGAR, which 'backing' places behind VIN.
explanation.definitionFit: This acidic condiment is soured wine, and its name comes from French for sour wine.

clue.text: Silly goon excluded from moving agony column's hatchet job

indicators.note: silly says the letters of goon can come out in any order, not as spelt
moving means rearranging, so the letters of agony column are shuffled
excluded from says the jumbled goon letters are removed from the pool

explanation.surface: A daft columnist cut from a touching advice page writes a vicious piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excluded from' takes G, O, O, N out of AGONY COLUMN; 'moving' rearranges the remaining ACLMNUY.
explanation.definitionFit: Calumny is a malicious false statement meant to damage reputation, a hatchet job in words.

clue.text: Small coin journalist got wind of

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes
a cent is a small coin
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter sniffs out a story worth very little.
explanation.definitionFit: To get wind of something is to sense or smell it out, as an animal catches a scent.
